entities.summary:
Zuane Pizzigano, a renowned 15th-century Venetian cartographer, left an indelible mark on the world of navigation and exploration. His 1424 portolan chart, the first known to depict the phantom islands of the purported Antillia archipelago, in the north Atlantic Ocean, sparked a wave of maritime discovery that would shape the course of European history.

 Pizzigano's chart not only showcased his expertise in astronomical cartography but also demonstrated his understanding of the complex interplay between geography, politics, and trade. By accurately mapping the island chain, he opened up new opportunities for Venetian merchants and sailors, who would go on to establish a vast network of trade routes across the Atlantic.

 The significance of Pizzigano's chart extends beyond its historical context, as it highlights the critical role of cartography in shaping the modern world. The chart's depiction of the Antillia archipelago, a concept that was later discredited by European explorers, serves as a powerful reminder of the complexities and uncertainties of historical cartography.

 In the realm of cultural heritage, Pizzigano's work continues to inspire artists, writers, and historians, who are drawn to the chart's intricate illustrations and poetic descriptions of the island chain. Today, the 1424 portolan chart is considered one of the most important navigational tools of the Renaissance, and its study remains a vital part of the history of cartography and exploration.
